specAnchors.text: understand that fertilisation involves the fusion of a male and female gamete to produce a zygote that undergoes cell division and develops into an embryo

primer.text: Every human starts as a single cell built from two half-cells. This note introduces the gametes — sperm and ovum — with the adaptations that help each one win its race or feed its passenger, then follows fertilisation from the oviduct meeting to the zygote's first mitotic divisions toward an embryo.

modules.title: The Sex Cells and Their Adaptations
modules.opening: Gametes are the sex cells made by meiosis, holding half the normal chromosome count: sperm swim with a tail and burn mitochondrial fuel, while the ovum sits rich in cytoplasm packed with energy stores for the early embryo.
keyPoints: Gametes are sex cells produced by meiosis: sperm and ovum in animals, pollen nucleus and ovum in plants.
Gametes contain half the number of chromosomes of normal body cells — 23 in human gametes.
Sperm have a tail to propel them and mitochondria supplying energy for movement.
Egg cells hold energy stores in their cytoplasm to support early embryo development.

low.restatement: Sperm travel light with a tail and an engine; eggs stay put but carry a packed lunch for the embryo.
low.analogy: A motorcycle courier racing to a delivery, and a depot stocked for the month after arrival.
low.examPointer: Quote the haploid count — 23 in humans — and tie each adaptation to its function.

medium.restatement: Meiosis halves the chromosome set so fertilisation can restore it; the tail and mitochondria exist because reaching the ovum is a competition, while the cytoplasmic reserves exist because the zygote must grow before any placenta supplies it.
medium.analogy: One cell arrives as a swimmer, the other waits as a supply drop.
medium.examPointer: Link adaptation to chance of successful fertilisation — that phrase earns the marks.

modules.title: Fertilisation and the First Divisions
modules.opening: Fertilisation is the fusion of a male and a female gamete into a zygote: sperm deposited near the cervix swim up, meet the egg in the oviduct, and the restored 46-chromosome cell divides by mitosis into a specialised embryo.
keyPoints: Fertilisation is the fusion of a male gamete and a female gamete to produce a zygote.
In humans the sperm meets the egg in the oviduct, typically one to two days after ovulation.
The zygote holds the full 46 chromosomes, half from each parent.
The zygote divides by mitosis and its cells specialise into an embryo's body tissues.

low.restatement: Two half-cells fuse into one whole cell, which then copies itself repeatedly and specialises into an embryo.
low.analogy: Two half-sheets of paper joined into one full sheet, then photocopied into a growing stack.
low.examPointer: Use the word fusion and name the zygote as the product — both are on the spec line.

medium.restatement: The oviduct meeting point matters because the egg is short-lived; after fusion, mitosis copies the restored genome so every descendant cell carries the full 46, and differentiation then assigns those copies to tissue jobs.
medium.analogy: Two keys cut to half a lock each click together and open the safe; then the safe starts printing itself.
medium.examPointer: Say mitosis for the divisions after fusion — meiosis made the gametes, mitosis grows the embryo.

glossary.definition: A sex cell carrying half the normal chromosome number, produced by meiosis.
The single cell formed when a male and female gamete fuse at fertilisation.
The tube between ovary and uterus where fertilisation usually occurs.
The early stage of development formed as the zygote divides by mitosis.
